target: Yo paso mucho tiempo en el carro.
english: I spend a lot of time in the car.
tip: Two spends: time is passed – 'paso mucho tiempo' – money is spent (gastar). Gastar tiempo sounds like wasting it.

target: Es normal estar nervioso el primer día.
english: It's normal to be nervous on the first day.
tip: Both verbs share this sentence: es normal states a general truth, so ser; estar nervioso marks a temporary state – the nerves will pass, so estar.

target: ¿Quieres que te ayude con la mudanza?
english: Do you want me to help you with the move?
tip: Why ayude, not ayudo? After quieres que, the helping is only wished-for, not yet real – Spanish marks unreal events with the subjunctive's flipped -e ending.

target: Los padres de mi novio son encantadores.
english: My boyfriend's parents are lovely.
tip: No apostrophe-s exists: 'los padres de mi novio' = the parents OF my boyfriend. Flip English possessives around de – the owner comes last.

target: En febrero los días son más cortos.
english: In February the days are shorter.
tip: 'Los días' – día ends in -a yet is masculine, alongside el mapa and el problema. A small club of -a masculines everyone trips on once.

target: Le hace ilusión ver a sus nietos.
english: He's excited about seeing his grandchildren.
tip: Built like gustar: the real subject is ver a sus nietos – the seeing 'makes ilusión,' and le just marks who receives the thrill. The excited person is never the subject.

target: Mi hermano juega al fútbol los sábados.
english: My brother plays soccer on Saturdays.
tip: Jugar demands a: 'juega AL fútbol' – literally plays TO the soccer, article included. Bare 'jugar fútbol' sounds off in Spain.

target: El gato come tres veces al día.
english: The cat eats three times a day.
tip: 'Tres veces al día' – literally 'to the day'. Spanish rates lean on al / a la: al día, a la semana, where English says per.

target: Ella entiende todo pero no dice nada.
english: She understands everything but doesn't say anything.
tip: 'No dice nada' – two negatives, and that's the correct form. Spanish demands the double: no before the verb, nada after. Bare 'dice nada' is broken.

target: Mi hija se duerme en el carro.
english: My daughter falls asleep in the car.
tip: That 'se' changes the verb: dormir = to sleep, dormirse = to FALL asleep. 'Se duerme en el carro' – she drifts off, not just sleeps.

target: ¡Hola! Me llamo María, encantada de conocerte.
english: Hello! My name is María, nice to meet you.
tip: Encantada ends in -a because María is the one speaking – this 'delighted' agrees with the speaker's own gender. A man introducing himself says encantado.

target: Eres la persona más puntual del equipo.
english: You are the most punctual person on the team.
tip: After a superlative, English 'in' turns into de: la más puntual DEL equipo – of the team. 'En el equipo' is the instinct; de is the rule.

target: Prefiero viajar en tren que en avión.
english: I prefer to travel by train rather than by plane.
tip: By train = 'en tren' – bare noun, no article: en tren, en avión, en autobús. Walking is the odd one out: a pie.

target: El próximo viernes es el primero de mes.
english: Next Friday is the first of the month.
tip: Spanish dates use plain numbers – el dos, el quince – with one exception: the 1st. El primero is the only ordinal allowed on the calendar, exactly as in this sentence.

target: No sé dónde está la estación de tren.
english: I don't know where the train station is.
tip: A place, yet sé not conozco: where the station is counts as a fact, and facts belong to saber. Conocer la estación would mean you've actually been there.

target: Mi hija pide helado después de cada comida.
english: My daughter asks for ice cream after every meal.
tip: 'Pide helado' – pedir already means ask FOR, so no extra word. Preguntar is only for asking questions. Spanish splits 'ask' in two.

target: Cruza la calle por el paso de peatones.
english: Cross the street at the crosswalk.
tip: Cruza looks exactly like 'he/she crosses' – because it is that form. Affirmative tú commands borrow the él/ella present; only the missing subject tells you it's an order.

target: Soy de España pero vivo en México ahora.
english: I'm from Spain but I live in Mexico now.
tip: 'Ser' + de expresses origin. 'Soy de España' = I'm from Spain. Use 'vivir en' for where you live now.

target: Mi abuelo es viudo.
english: My grandfather is a widower.
tip: Ser for civil status: "Es soltero." Marital status uses ser – it defines identity, not a passing state.

target: Hace un cuarto de hora que espero el autobús.
english: I've been waiting for the bus for a quarter of an hour.
tip: 'Hace + time + que + present tense' expresses duration: 'Hace un cuarto de hora que te espero' = I've been waiting for you for fifteen minutes.

target: ¿Tienes hijos? Sí, tengo un hijo y una hija.
english: Do you have children? Yes, I have a son and a daughter.
tip: '¿Tienes hijos?' keeps statement word order – Spanish yes/no questions often do; intonation does the work.

target: ¿Quieres el filete poco hecho, al punto o bien hecho?
english: Do you want the steak rare, medium, or well done?
tip: Steak doneness: 'poco hecho' (barely done) = rare, 'al punto' (at the point) = medium, 'bien hecho' = well done – the standard terms waiters use.

target: Estoy bien, gracias.
english: I am fine, thanks.
tip: 'Estoy' is estar – used for temporary states, like how you feel right now.

target: ¿Tiene usted reserva?
english: Do you have a reservation?
tip: Usted – formal you, used in service contexts and with strangers.

target: La cena está lista.
english: Dinner is ready.
tip: Está lista = dinner's ready, but es lista = she's smart. With some adjectives, ser vs estar changes the meaning, not just the timing.

target: Nosotros somos de España.
english: We are from Spain.
tip: Somos alone already says 'we are' – so why nosotros? Spanish drops subject pronouns, and keeping one adds weight: WE are from Spain, whatever the rest of you are.

target: Extraño a mi familia.
english: I miss my family.
tip: Missing someone? 'Extraño' is the Latin American verb; in Spain you'd hear 'echo de menos a mi familia.' Same feeling, different phrase – pick your side of the Atlantic.

target: Estamos en el aeropuerto.
english: We're at the airport.
tip: Estar for location: "Está en Madrid." Physical position always uses estar (except events).

target: Esta comida está deliciosa.
english: This food is delicious.
tip: Estar for taste/experience: "La sopa está rica." How something tastes/seems right now → estar.

target: La puerta está abierta.
english: The door is open.
tip: Estar for resulting states: "Está roto." The door isn't broken by nature – it became broken. Result of change → estar.
